title: No Defects Found in AI-171 Fuel Switch as India's Crash Probe Nears Completion
excerpt: Boeing's examination of the fuel control switch found no abnormalities, but evaluation of the full Thrust Control Module continues at the manufacturer's Seattle facility, India's aviation minister told Parliament during the Monsoon Session.
body:
• Tests by Boeing found no defects in the fuel control switch of the crashed Air India AI-171 Boeing 787-8, Minister of State Murlidhar Mohol told Parliament.
  • The AAIB investigation into the June 2025 Ahmedabad crash that killed 260 people is now in its final stages, with the final report to be published online.
  • A separate February 2026 incident on another Air India 787-8 — where a fuel switch slipped from RUN to CUTOFF with minimal pressure — also showed no abnormality after Boeing testing.
  • The complete Thrust Control Module from the February incident is being evaluated at Boeing's Seattle facility, with results still pending.

India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau is in the final stages of its probe into the Air India AI-171 crash that killed 260 people in Ahmedabad in June 2025, Minister of State for Civil Aviation Murlidhar Mohol told Parliament this week. Tests by Boeing, the original equipment manufacturer, found no defects in the 787-8 Dreamliner's fuel control switch — a component at the heart of the investigation — though evaluation of the broader thrust control system continues at Boeing's Seattle facility.

What Boeing's Tests Revealed

Mohol, responding to questions during the Monsoon Session, said a detailed examination of the fuel control switch, including its locking detents and structural integrity, found no abnormality.

"A detailed examination of the fuel control switch, including the structural integrity of its locking detents, found no abnormality."

— Murlidhar Mohol, Minister of State for Civil Aviation

The tests were ordered by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation as part of continuing airworthiness checks after the agency grounded the Boeing 787-8 type in February 2026, according to Outlook Business.

The fuel control switch has been the focal point of the investigation since the AAIB's preliminary report, released in July 2025, established that both engine fuel control switches on Flight AI-171 transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF seconds after takeoff on June 12, 2025. The Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, bound for London Gatwick, crashed 32 seconds after liftoff into the densely populated Meghani Nagar area near Ahmedabad's Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport. It was the first fatal crash in the history of the 787.

A Second Fuel Switch Incident

The fuel switch issue resurfaced in February 2026 when pilots on an Air India Boeing 787-8 flying from London Heathrow to Bengaluru filed a Pilot Defect Report flagging that a fuel control switch slipped from RUN to CUTOFF with minimal pressure. The Ministry of Civil Aviation confirmed the switch failed to lock positively in its selected position.

Air India grounded the aircraft, and Boeing conducted inspections and functional tests. The manufacturer classified the unit as "mechanically functioning as designed" and serviceable. A fuel control switch from the aircraft was dispatched to the United States for further testing, according to Aviation A2Z. The aircraft returned to service within days.

Boeing has since found no abnormality in that switch either, Reuters reported, citing Mohol's statement to Parliament. The complete Thrust Control Module from the February incident is now being evaluated at Boeing's facility in Seattle.

Legal Pressure and Competing Theories

The investigation has faced mounting legal and public scrutiny. The Safety Matters Foundation, an aviation safety NGO, filed a public interest litigation in the Supreme Court in September 2025 seeking an independent, court-monitored probe. The plea alleged the AAIB's preliminary report suppressed critical data from the Digital Flight Data Recorder, Cockpit Voice Recorder, and Electronic Aircraft Fault Recording systems while prematurely suggesting pilot error.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta defended the investigation's timeline in court, citing the complexity of dispatching components abroad for testing.

"This is not like some in-house investigation here."

— Tushar Mehta, Solicitor General of India

Two theories continue to divide the aviation community. One camp, backed by pilot associations and Indian Air Force veterans, points to an electrical failure that may have triggered the Ram Air Turbine deployment within seconds of liftoff. The Safety Matters Foundation has cited four indicators from the preliminary report — absence of a speed data source, powerless boom microphones, internal melting of the tail box, and landing gear freezing mid-retraction — as evidence of electrical failure.

The opposing theory attributes the fuel switch movement to deliberate pilot action, a claim rejected by pilot groups. The cockpit voice recording captured one pilot asking the other why he cut the fuel; the other denied having done so. India's Supreme Court noted that the preliminary report carries "no insinuation against the pilot."

Diaspora Connections

The crash claimed lives across the Indian diaspora, including passengers bound for the United Kingdom. Among the dead was former Gujarat Chief Minister Vijay Rupani. The investigation's outcome could carry regulatory implications for Boeing 787 operations worldwide, affecting routes heavily used by diaspora travellers between India, the UK, and other destinations. The aircraft type's grounding and airworthiness checks have already disrupted Air India's long-haul fleet operations.

What's Next

The government rejected claims that the AAIB had delayed its final report, stating that major air accident investigations do not follow fixed timelines. "All probable causes and contributing factors leading to the accident are being investigated," Mohol told Parliament. The AAIB will publish its final report online once the probe is complete. Investigators are still awaiting Boeing's evaluation of the Thrust Control Module in Seattle — results that could prove decisive in resolving whether the fuel switch movement was caused by a mechanical fault or human action.
